# Life is Hard and Undecidable, but...

Life is Hard and Undecidable, but...
Input file: standard input
Output file: standard output
Time limit: 1 second
Memory limit: 1024 megabytes
To John Horton Conway, his Game of Life, and also the life we are living...
Disclaimer: For those who have no patience for the whole context or are already familiar
with Game of Life, the problem is in the last paragraph on the third page.
Life is hard. There are beautiful dreams, yet you can never realize them. There are regrets and lost loved
ones, yet you can never turn back time. There is death lying ahead with the anxiety it persistently gives
you, yet you have no way to escape from it. There are problems right here for you to solve, yet you simply
don’t know how.
Life is hard.
Life is undecidable. You just don’t know what you are going to get from this box of chocolates. Experienced
through all the Black Swan and Grey Rhino events happening those years, we all wonder, what’s going
to happen next? What will the future be like? “C’est la vie”, say the old folks. It goes to show you never
can tell.
But, life just goes on. We have wines to drink, songs to sing, problems to solve, and games to play. The
game we will play now is, Game of Life, or simply, Life, devised by the famous British mathematician
John Horton Conway in 1970.
Life is a zero-player “game” played on an infinite squared board. At any time, some of the cells will be
live and others dead. Which cells are live at generation 0 is up to you! But then you’ve got nothing else
to do because the state at any later time is determined by the previous one by the following rules:
• BIRTH. A cell that’s dead at generation t becomes live at generation t + 1 if and only if exactly
three of its eight neighbors were live at generation t.
• DEATH by overcrowding. A cell that’s live at generation t becomes dead at generation t + 1 if
at least four of its eight neighbors were live at generation t.
• DEATH by exposure. A cell that’s live at generation t becomes dead at generation t + 1 if at
most one of its eight neighbors were live at generation t.
• Survival. A cell that’s live at generation t is still live at generation t + 1 if two or three of its eight
neighbors were live at generation t.
The rule above can be summarized and memorized as “Just 3 for birth, 2 or 3 for survival.”
The following picture is an example of starting from a configuration where only five cells in a line are live.
This will end up forming a “traffic light” pattern that repeats infinitely with a period of 2. In the picture,
filled circles represent live cells that will still be live at the next generation. Unfilled circles represent
live cells that will be dead at the next generation. Dots represent dead cells that will be live at the next
generation. (Credit: All pictures below are from Winning Ways For Your Mathematical Plays, Volume 4
by Elwyn R. Berlekamp and John H. Conway).
Page 1 of 3

A Line of five becomes traffic lights.
There are some other examples of starting configurations with different “destinies":
Different start, different destiny.
There are examples where one ends up in a life cycle,
Three life cycles with period 2.
and an example of a moving “glider".
A glider moving diagonally.
Page 2 of 3

Mathematicians and theoretical computer scientists are fascinated by the mystery of Life. They ask the
following question: “Given a starting configuration of Life, can we decide if it will eventually die out?
i.e., is there some finite number t such that there is no live cells at generation t?” However, it turns out
this problem is not only NP-hard, but even undecidable. It is possible to build a pattern in Life that
acts like a finite-state machine connected to two counters. This has the same computational power as a
universal Turing machine, so Life is theoretically as powerful as any computer with unlimited memory and
no time constraints; it is Turing complete. In fact, several different programmable computer architectures
have been implemented in Life, including a pattern that simulates Tetris.
Although as the above suggests, we can never unravel the mystery of Life, there are still certain things
we can do. Construction is just one of those things, and is also exactly what this problem asks for:
Given a positive integer k (1 ≤ k ≤ 100), construct a starting configuration of Game of Life,
with all live cells having positive coordinates not exceeding 300, so that the configuration
lasts exactly k generations, that is, there exist live cells at generation k − 1, but no live cells
at generation k. It is guaranteed that at least one such starting configuration exists.
Input
The input consists of only one integer k (1 ≤ k ≤ 100), denoting the number of generations the
configuration need to last.
Output
The first line contains an integer n, (1 ≤ n ≤ 90000), denoting the number of live cells in your starting
configuration.
Then n lines follow, each line containing two integers x, y (1 ≤ x, y ≤ 300), denoting the coordinates of a
live cell in your starting configuration. The coordinates of each live cell should be output exactly once.
If there are many possible starting configurations, outputting any of them will be considered correct.
Examples
standard input standard output
1 1
1 1
2 3
100 100
101 100
102 99
Page 3 of 3

[PDF](https://codeforces.com/gym/104065/problem/H)

# Life is Hard and Undecidable, but...

## Description

To John Horton Conway, his Game of Life, and also the life we are living...

**Disclaimer:** If you have no patience for the full context or already know Game of Life, the actual task is in the last paragraph on the third page of the original PDF.

Life is hard. There are beautiful dreams you can never realize. There are regrets and lost loved ones, yet you cannot turn back time. There is death ahead, with the anxiety it persistently gives you, yet you cannot escape it. There are problems right here for you to solve, yet you simply do not know how.

![Original figure](104065-H-figure1.png)

Life is hard.

Life is undecidable. You never know what you are going to get from this box of chocolates. Having experienced all the Black Swan and Grey Rhino events over the years, we all wonder what happens next and what the future will be like. “C'est la vie”, say the old folks. It goes to show you never can tell.

But life goes on. We have wines to drink, songs to sing, problems to solve, and games to play. Our game now is Game of Life, or simply Life, devised by the famous British mathematician John Horton Conway in 1970.

Life is a zero-player game on an infinite square grid. Every cell is either alive or dead. You choose which cells are alive in generation $0$; after that, the state of each generation is completely determined by the previous generation using these rules:

- **Birth:** a cell dead at generation $t$ becomes alive at generation $t+1$ if and only if exactly $3$ of its $8$ neighbors were alive at generation $t$.
- **Death by overcrowding:** a cell alive at generation $t$ becomes dead at generation $t+1$ if at least $4$ of its $8$ neighbors were alive at generation $t$.
- **Death by exposure:** a cell alive at generation $t$ becomes dead at generation $t+1$ if at most $1$ of its $8$ neighbors was alive at generation $t$.
- **Survival:** a cell alive at generation $t$ remains alive at generation $t+1$ if $2$ or $3$ of its $8$ neighbors were alive at generation $t$.

The rules can be remembered as “Just $3$ for birth, $2$ or $3$ for survival.”

The following example starts with only five live cells in a line and eventually becomes a traffic-light pattern repeating with period $2$. Filled circles denote live cells that remain alive in the next generation; unfilled circles denote live cells that die in the next generation; dots denote dead cells that become alive in the next generation. All the following pictures are from Winning Ways for Your Mathematical Plays, Volume $4$, by Elwyn R. Berlekamp and John H. Conway.

![Original figure](104065-H-figure2.png)

A line of five becomes traffic lights.

Here are other starting configurations with different destinies:

![Original figure](104065-H-figure3.png)

Different starts, different destinies.

Some starting configurations enter a repeating life cycle:

![Original figure](104065-H-figure4.png)

Three life cycles with period $2$.

Another example is a moving glider:

![Original figure](104065-H-figure5.png)

A glider moving diagonally.

Mathematicians and theoretical computer scientists are fascinated by Life. They ask: given a starting configuration, can we determine whether it will eventually die out, that is, whether there is some finite generation $t$ with no live cells? This problem is not only NP-hard but even undecidable. A pattern in Life can act as a finite-state machine connected to two counters. Such a machine has the same computational power as a universal Turing machine. Thus Life is theoretically as powerful as a computer with unlimited memory and time: it is Turing complete. Several programmable computer architectures have been implemented in Life, including a pattern that simulates Tetris.

Although this suggests that we can never unravel every mystery of Life, there are still things we can do. Construction is one of them, and is exactly what this task asks for:

Given a positive integer $k$ ($1\le k\le100$), construct an initial configuration with every live cell having positive coordinates at most $300$, so that it lasts exactly $k$ generations: generation $k-1$ has at least one live cell, while generation $k$ has none. At least one such configuration is guaranteed to exist.

## Input

The input consists of one integer $k$ ($1\le k\le100$), the required number of generations.

## Output

First output an integer $n$ ($1\le n\le90000$), the number of live cells in the initial configuration.

Then output $n$ lines, each containing two integers $x,y$ ($1\le x,y\le300$), the coordinates of one initial live cell. Output each cell exactly once. Any valid configuration is accepted.

### Sample 1

#### Input

```text
1
```

#### Output

```text
1
1 1
```

### Sample 2

#### Input

```text
2
```

#### Output

```text
3
100 100
101 100
102 99
```

translation.markdown:
# Life is Hard and Undecidable, but...

## 题目描述

献给 John Horton Conway、他的生命游戏，以及我们正在经历的人生……

**提示：** 如果你没有耐心阅读完整背景，或者已经了解生命游戏，可直接阅读原 PDF 第三页最后一段的实际任务。

人生艰难。有些美好的梦想，你永远无法实现。有些遗憾和失去的挚爱，你却无法让时光倒流。死亡就在前方，持续带来焦虑，你却无法逃避。有些问题就摆在面前等待你解决，你却完全不知道该怎么办。

![原稿配图](104065-H-figure1.png)

人生艰难。

人生不可判定。你永远不知道会从这盒巧克力里得到什么。经历了这些年的黑天鹅与灰犀牛事件，我们都在想：接下来会发生什么，未来又会怎样？正如长者所说，“这就是生活”（C'est la vie）。未来总是难以预料。

但生活仍要继续。我们有酒可饮，有歌可唱，有题可做，有游戏可玩。接下来要玩的就是生命游戏（Game of Life，简称 Life），它由著名英国数学家 John Horton Conway 于 1970 年提出。

生命游戏是在无限方格网格上进行的零玩家游戏。每个格子要么存活，要么死亡。第 $0$ 代哪些格子存活由你决定；之后不再需要操作，每一代的状态完全由上一代按以下规则确定：

- **诞生：** 第 $t$ 代死亡的格子，当且仅当它的 $8$ 个邻居中恰好有 $3$ 个在第 $t$ 代存活时，才会在第 $t+1$ 代存活。
- **拥挤致死：** 第 $t$ 代存活的格子，若它的 $8$ 个邻居中至少有 $4$ 个在第 $t$ 代存活，则会在第 $t+1$ 代死亡。
- **孤独致死：** 第 $t$ 代存活的格子，若它的 $8$ 个邻居中至多有 $1$ 个在第 $t$ 代存活，则会在第 $t+1$ 代死亡。
- **存活：** 第 $t$ 代存活的格子，若它的 $8$ 个邻居中有 $2$ 或 $3$ 个在第 $t$ 代存活，则会在第 $t+1$ 代继续存活。

以上规则可以记作：“恰有 $3$ 个邻居时诞生，有 $2$ 或 $3$ 个邻居时存活。”

下面的例子从排成一行的五个存活格子开始，最终变成一个周期为 $2$ 的“交通灯”图案。实心圆表示这一代存活且下一代仍存活的格子；空心圆表示这一代存活但下一代死亡的格子；小点表示这一代死亡但下一代存活的格子。以下所有插图均出自 Elwyn R. Berlekamp 与 John H. Conway 的《Winning Ways for Your Mathematical Plays》第 $4$ 卷。

![原稿配图](104065-H-figure2.png)

一行五个存活格子演变为交通灯。

其他初始状态也会有不同的结局：

![原稿配图](104065-H-figure3.png)

不同的开始，不同的命运。

有些初始状态会进入循环：

![原稿配图](104065-H-figure4.png)

三种周期为 $2$ 的循环。

还有会移动的“滑翔机”：

![原稿配图](104065-H-figure5.png)

沿对角线移动的滑翔机。

数学家和理论计算机科学家对生命游戏的奥秘着迷。他们提出：给定一个初始状态，能否判断它最终是否会完全消亡，也就是是否存在有限的某一代 $t$，使所有格子都死亡？这个问题不只是 NP-hard，甚至是不可判定的。生命游戏中的某些图案可以模拟连接两个计数器的有限状态机，而这样的机器具有与通用图灵机相同的计算能力。因此，生命游戏在理论上与具有无限内存和无限运行时间的计算机一样强大，即它是图灵完备的。人们已在生命游戏中实现了多种可编程计算机体系结构，甚至包括能模拟俄罗斯方块的图案。

虽然这意味着我们无法解开生命游戏的所有谜团，但仍然有些事情是可以做到的，其中之一就是构造。这正是本题要求你完成的：

给定一个正整数 $k$（$1\le k\le100$），请构造一个初始状态，要求所有存活格子的两个坐标均为不超过 $300$ 的正整数，并使该状态恰好持续 $k$ 代：第 $k-1$ 代仍有存活格子，第 $k$ 代则没有任何存活格子。保证至少存在一个满足条件的初始状态。

## 输入格式

输入仅包含一个整数 $k$（$1\le k\le100$），表示要求持续的代数。

## 输出格式

第一行输出一个整数 $n$（$1\le n\le90000$），表示初始状态中存活格子的数量。

接下来输出 $n$ 行，每行包含两个整数 $x,y$（$1\le x,y\le300$），表示一个初始存活格子的坐标。每个格子只能输出一次。存在多个合法初始状态时，输出任意一个即可。

### 样例 1

#### 输入

```text
1
```

#### 输出

```text
1
1 1
```

### 样例 2

#### 输入

```text
2
```

#### 输出

```text
3
100 100
101 100
102 99
```

notes: All three original pages and every diagram reviewed visually. All five original pictures retained, with explanatory captions translated.
Generation 0 is the chosen initial state; generation k-1 must be nonempty and generation k empty. The 300 bound applies to initial live coordinates, not an artificial finite board boundary.
Historical long-form background and source illustration credit retained; four Life rules checked separately.
